prompt: Insertion sort on n items takes `Θ(n)` time on already-sorted input and `Θ(n^2)` time on reverse-sorted input (Θ means "grows at exactly this rate, up to constants"). Which statement about its running time over **all** inputs of size n is correct?

options.explanation: This is the worst-case tight bound, not a uniform tight bound for every input: sorted input is linear.
Only the best case has a tight linear bound. Reverse-sorted input performs roughly half the square of the item count.

options.text: It is O(n), because Big-O describes the best case
options.explanation: Big-O does not mean 'best case' (or 'worst case'). O, Ω and Θ are bounds on functions; best/worst/average say which inputs the function describes.
Correct. Every input has a quadratic upper bound and a linear lower bound, but the input cases do not share one tight bound.

workedExample: Sorted input establishes a linear best-case function; reverse-sorted distinct input establishes a quadratic worst-case function. Every input lies between those extremes. Thus all inputs share the linear lower and quadratic upper bounds, but there is no uniform tight growth bound in item count n alone.

prompt: A function does `n` steps when n is even and `1` step when n is odd, where n is a positive whole number (the input size). Which statements about its running time `f(n)` are true? Select all that apply.

options.explanation: True. On even sizes the cost equals the input size; on odd sizes it is smaller. A linear upper bound covers both.
True. Every value is at least one, so the function has a constant lower bound.
False. On odd inputs the constant cost eventually breaks every proposed positive linear lower multiplier.
False, for the same reason: the odd values keep dropping to 1, so no positive c works for all large n.
False. The even inputs use one step per item, so no fixed constant upper bound works for all large inputs; n is item count.

workedExample: Check both infinite subsequences. Even sizes keep increasing and defeat a constant upper bound. Odd sizes stay at one and defeat a positive linear lower bound. The cost is always between one and the input size n, so the constant lower and linear upper bounds remain valid.
